description: Tôi cần những người nghiêm túc, trách nhiệm.
summary: Space Mission Design Simulator is a free, browser-based game that lets kids and beginners design real-style space missions to all seven other planets of the Solar System. Players build a spacecraft from 26 parts, launch it, steer it through an asteroid field, and run the mission year by year while handling dust storms, radiation and power failures. Every choice is a trade-off between six resources: budget, mass, energy, communication, data storage and lifespan, plus fuel. Distances, sunlight and signal strength follow simple real physics and NASA planetary data, so players discover why a Jupiter probe needs a bigger antenna or why Mars dust storms threaten solar panels. Guided by Bob and his AI companion LUMI, players learn that failure is part of engineering: check the report, change one part and try again.
details:
What does it do?

The game turns spacecraft engineering into a hands-on puzzle. The player is a young mission designer, Bob, working with LUMI (Learn · Universe · Mission · Intelligence), a friendly AI assistant. Together they fly to Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Each planet has three missions (21 in total): a flyby, an orbiter, and a special mission such as a Mars communication relay, a Venus radar map, a Jupiter atmospheric probe, an icy-moon probe at Saturn, or a Grand Tour at Neptune.

Each mission follows the same flow that real teams use:

  1. Briefing – the goal, the planet's environment (heat, radiation, dust, impacts) and the budget.
  2. Assembly – drag or tap parts from seven groups (power, communication, control, science, protection, storage, propulsion) onto a hull. A live dashboard shows how each part changes every resource.
  3. Launch – choose a launcher that can lift the total mass.
  4. Flight – steer through hazards; a pilot-assist mode helps younger players.
  5. Mission control – the simulation runs year by year. Events appear only when the design is truly at its limit (low energy, unshielded radiation, dust storms, collisions), and the player picks a response with visible consequences.
  6. Report – a score, stars and rewards that explain what went well and what to improve.

After each world, the player unlocks a page of the Solar System Discovery Notebook with a "Did you know?" fact. Completing all seven pages finishes the story. There is also research, 20 achievements, a tutorial, four budget levels (from relaxed to free play), and full Vietnamese/English language support.

How does it work?

The core is a deterministic resource calculator: the same design always gives the same result, so players can test ideas fairly. It uses school-level physics that real mission designers also start from:

  • Sunlight and solar-panel output fall with the square of the distance from the Sun. At Mars a panel gets about 43% of the light it gets at Earth; at Jupiter only a few percent.
  • Radio signal strength falls with the square of the distance to Earth, so outer-planet missions need larger antennas and more data storage.
  • Planet distances come from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet. Heat, radiation and dust are converted into simple 0–3 levels so kids can read them.

Fuel, engine and cost numbers are abstract game units, chosen so the trade-offs stay realistic in direction but easy to understand. A built-in solver checks that every mission can be solved in unlock order, so the game is challenging but never impossible.

What benefits does it have?

  • Learning by doing: players experience systems engineering and trade-offs instead of memorising facts.
  • Safe failure: a failed mission comes with a clear report, which builds resilience and a scientific mindset.
  • Accessible: runs in any modern browser on laptop, tablet or phone, with no installation, no account and no internet after loading. Progress is saved locally on the device.
  • Bilingual: Vietnamese and English, so it can be used in Vietnamese classrooms and internationally.
  • Easy to extend: all planets, parts, missions and events live in simple data files, so teachers or students can add new content without changing code.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want children aged about 9–14 to feel that designing a space mission is something they can do. We hope teachers use the game in science lessons about the Solar System, and that players come away curious about real NASA missions such as Voyager, Juno, Cassini and Perseverance. Next steps: test with classmates and younger students, add teacher worksheets, and include more NASA mission stories in the notebook.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES Modules), no framework and no backend
  • Graphics drawn in code (SVG and Canvas); sound effects synthesised with the Web Audio API, no image or audio files
  • Node.js test runner (unit tests) and Playwright (browser tests at phone, tablet and desktop sizes)
  • esbuild for packaging; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting
  • An AI coding assistant (see Use of Artificial Intelligence)

Use of NASA Data & Resources

  • NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (NSSDCA,https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/): average distance of each planet from the Sun and the minimum and maximum distance from Earth. These numbers drive the solar-power and communication calculations, so they directly shape every spacecraft design.
  • NASA Solar System Exploration (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/): planet facts used in the story and the "Did you know?" cards, for example Olympus Mons being about 22 km tall, a Mars day lasting 24 h 37 min, Jupiter rotating in about 10 hours, Uranus's 42-year polar day and night, and Neptune's 165-year orbit.
  • Real NASA missions inspired the mission types: flybys (Mariner, Voyager), orbiters (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Juno, Cassini), radar mapping of Venus (Magellan), atmospheric probes (Galileo probe) and communication relays at Mars.

The game does not use NASA logos or claim any NASA endorsement.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Yes, we used AI, and we want to be clear about how.

  • Code: most of the game code was written by Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, following the game design, rules and requests written by our team. We reviewed the results by playing, reported problems, and asked for changes many times.
  • Text: the AI helped draft and polish the story dialogue for Bob and LUMI, the team introduction and the English translation, based on the story ideas and planet choices from our team.
  • Graphics and sound: no AI image, video or voice generators were used. All pictures are drawn by code and all sounds are synthesised in the browser.
  • What the team did: game idea and design, mission list, story concept and characters, finding and checking NASA facts, playtesting and difficulty balancing, and final decisions on everything in the game.
  • Inside the game: LUMI is a fictional character. The game does not call any AI service while you play and does not collect player data.

References

  • NASA Planetary Fact Sheet – https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
  • NASA Science: Solar System – https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/
  • Claude Code (AI coding assistant) – https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code
  • Playwright – https://playwright.dev
  • esbuild – https://esbuild.github.io
